comments.text: @glamdring0007  FSR2 is so far behind DLSS in actual quality it's not even worth comparing the two in terms of quality to performance. As someone who has used both forms of upscaling extensively I can say FSR2 even with the Quality preset in its current form introduces a ton of artifacts in high motion scenes, bad ghosting, poor original texture retention, and an all around grainy look. These are all things that DLSS2 also running on the Quality preset do not suffer from, visually no matter if they're high motion scenes or stagnated ones you'll be hard pressed to find any noticeable differences between running natively or using DLSS2 Quality outside of the significant boost in frame rate. This is the power of AI upscaling and it's the same reason AMD needs to announce AI powered FSR3 during the announcement today on 7000 series Radeon cards. If they still haven't implemented machine learning on RDNA3 they're going to be significantly behind the curve as the industry is slowly moving away from the importance of pure rasterization performance. Even the Arc A770 at $349 has machine learning technology on it that is quite frankly very good for a 1st generation card. I'd love to move over to Radeon GPUs, but in their current state they're lacking an obscene amount of QoL features and support for workloads outside of gaming that simply makes them less desirable. These are the same reasons hardware surveys show that in the professional workspace Radeon is virtually non-existent, and in the PC gaming space a lowly 17% of PC owners are running Radeon GPUs with Nvidia holding all of that other market share between the two sectors.

comments.text:
Only issue with the video is saying this replaces the 5700 XT.  You can't look at pricing to determine what replaces what because WAY different time.  It replaces the 5600 XT, and it should have been tested against the 5600 XT.

This is a good half year past this video, but what I'm ore excited to see is that prices are slowly coming down and I FINALLY see a high quality 6800 XT for around $1200 USD.  Consdiering they've been up at $1600 USD this is a good thing.  Not great, but a good thing.  I don't think they can come down much below $1000 - $1100 due to global inflation, not scalping which is raising the cost of manufacturing a GPU about 20% more expensive than 1.5 years ago, along with the 25% tariff on GPUs coming into the US.  That inflation is probably never going away because a lot of it is dealing with higher wages being paid out, and driving wages down is really hard, and it is too painful for people who make those wages because the economy adjusts to those higher wages, and other costs go up to take away those higher wages, such as housing costs, rent, etc...

So, if you see the 6800 XT near $1000 USD that's probably the best it's ever going to get.  If you want one, buy it then.  But if it's a higher quality product, don't expect it to drop under $1200, ever, such as a PowerColor Red Devil.

comments.text:
Disagree with this. I bought the 6600XT, at good price too, below MSRP, below even the 3060 MSRP, which was the reason why I pulled the trigger. The reason why the 6600XT is such a terrible card, isn't its performance, it's its price. In the a reasonable world, this card would be position at the same MSRP as the 3060. They trade blows, with the 3060 being faster on some games and 6600XT on others, due to the cut in memory interface. Yet, AMD priced it much higher, closer to the 3060Ti which destroyed it in almost all situations. 

Prices at 3060 MSRP, the 6600XT would have terrific value. It would beat the 3060 on many occasions, but with the trade-off, of having worse performance in streaming, no RT core and DLSS. That's something most people can live with. Even then, that's not a great look, if we don't account for the price inflation. That's because the performance per dollars improvement of the 3060 at MSRP isn't great either, but that card has the excuse of having RT, and perhaps DLSS. FSR is useable on all cards, so there's nothing that can excuse the 6600XT. Yet, AMD took advantage of the situation and brazenly placed the MSRP at $380, far beyond where it should have been. 

Someone mentioned in another video that it could have been a $250 card. That sounds extreme, but that's the level of improvement that makes sense in a normal market. At $250, it would be crushing NVIDIA offering, basically a slightly better 3060 without all the bells and whistles, at the no RT cost. $280 would make the most sense. $380 only makes sense in the inflated market, as GN described it "mid-range is dead". NVIDIA shot it in the face, and AMD gave it the last kick. I got the 6600XT at $300. That's $80 dollars off the MSRP, yet I can't help but feel bitter about buying at the price range I thought it should have been launched with. I can't help but wonder if consumers like me who purchase bad products at high prices is the reason why the market has gotten this bad. The 6600XT deserved all of the criticism, it being sold at below its MSRP, is exactly what it deserves. We didn't get a good deal, we just avoided getting screwed by AMD and NVIDIA.

comments.text: I'm going to start off by saying with this card on low settings I was getting on average over 100 frames a second at 8K in world of warships and my CPU is a ryzan 3600. War zone I was getting between 70 and 80 on average on low settings across the board except for cashe always got to have the cashe on in 4k. If I turn on dynamic resolution it jumps to well over 100. Also must let everybody know that this card makes almost every first and second gen rising a potential bottleneck pending on how you set the settings in game. The only time I was able to get 100% GPU usage was during benchmarks or when I had battlefield 2042 maxed out. When I went up to 4K it pretty much utilized the whole GPU but like I said my CPU became the bottleneck when as previously my RX 590 was the bottleneck. I got this GPU mainly for one thing because I was getting good FPS with my 590 across the board with almost any games as long as I tweak with it. VR encoding bottom line that is the only reason why I upgraded. This card can handle it. And say virtual desktop recommended would be medium settings with the 590 it was potato. Pending on what I'm playing on medium settings I'm getting $120 frames a second with settings on low. However if I bumped it up to ultra in virtual desktop and a lot of instances I was hitting 90 frames a second and as far as the streaming my only bottleneck was the actual game. The encoding the networking perfect. Previously the encoding on the 590 couldn't handle anything above potato which of course introduced latency but I always played on low tweeked settings anyways. This card is specifically designed to bump up to a whole nother generation above Vega and the 500 series. And works best with the ryzen 5000 series. Word of advice do not enable resizable bar unless you have a 5000 series CPU. Now with all that said maybe the top tier 3,000 series rising CPUs and Intel equivalents can utilize this card to its full potential at 1080p. But anything below that the CPU is a bottleneck and the only way you'll get full GPU utilization is bumping the resolution or Max settings or a mix of both. It's still a million times better than any AMD card of its class before it.

comments.text:
The problem with AMD RDNA is we have a great Architecture (and GPUs) essentially being made terrible by both Pricing but also Marketing on the Branding of each Variant.

Now personally instead of comparing Price Point., I compare GPU Size.
Why? Well because in general terms the same Die Size should be a similar Production Price... this isn't true going from N16 to N7. 

In general terms we're talking an increase of approx. 30% per mm in regards to cost, with N7P being a further 12% more expensive.
i.e. a 230mm N16 cost ~$58 / Unit., while a 230mm N7 likely costs ~$75 / Unit., and a 230mm N7P likely costing ~$84 / Unit.

Alright, so if we assume all components increased by said value (they didn't but, arguments sake we will).
RX 5700 XT • £380 ARP • £440 PNP • £290 ERP
As it stands., we're getting a +16% Better Performance for the same Price... but what we should've got was +52% Better Performance for the same Price. 
With pricing that matches the increase in production costs; suddenly the RX 5700 XT goes from a "eh, it's alright" to "awesome" 

And the same is true if we take this concept to the Next-Generation
RX 6700 XT • £480 ARP • £515 PNP • £325 ERP 
As it stands we're getting +7% Performance for the same Price... but what we should've got was +31% Performance for the same Price. 
Again... this is a notable shift from being a "It's a shame an RX 5800 didn't exist" to "this is a decent upgrade" 

What is a serious shame is that we have some of the best and most impressive architectures from both NVIDIA and AMD this generation., both ruined by Pricing.
And the ONLY reason NVIDIA initially got praise for the RTX 30-Series was because the RTX 20-Series was initially over-priced; which they cannibalised their own Product Stack with new SKU ("SUPER" Cards) to provide better value; as RDNA 1.0 had the potential (if AMD had bothered producing High-End Cards) to provide comparable performance at a better price-point.

(Even IF the RX 5000-Series were overpriced)

•

But you know the biggest losers in all of this are., are those with limited Funds.
There is a complete absence of the £100 - £180 Graphics Card Market... and this traditionally is 85% of the Gaming Market., with the "Sweet" Spot being £140 - £160...
AMD seem content in allowing their APUs to provide Graphics to this Segment of the Market; but the problem is that we're talking an absolute gulf in terms of a Performance Gap between the High-End APU (R9 5700G) and the Low-End GPU (RX 6600 XT) 

There is essentially NO Mainstream GPU Market now... as while the RX 6600 XT should be a Mainstream Mid-Range (£150 - 180) Graphics Card; it presently sits at £330... that's effective 2x where it SHOULD be in terms of price.

Now is it good value for RX 5700 XT owners like myself?
Eh., well I got mine for £380... and sure; for the same basic performance at £50 cheaper; that's not a complete loss; and the Lower TDP is also good, esp. for people concerned about their electricity bill or system thermals. 
My RX 5700 XT being a reference certainly likes to be heard when under load; and it also REALLY warms my room., so no need for Heating come Winter.

Still that's just not low enough for the Mainstream Market., and we are talking something that's an x60 Class Card; which is supposed to be Mainstream Low-to-Mid Range. 
And here's the kicker... by my estimations (as with the RX 5700 XT and RX 6700 XT); the RX 6600 XT should be £140 - £150... the sweet spot for what it is; and at that price, well suddenly rather than being "Meh" it would be a "Must Have" and "Exciting"

@abcplay57  Depends on what broke. For me it has always been the soldering between the GPU and the PCB that cracked from all the heating and cooling circles. Heating it up enough so that the soldering becomes liquid and letting it cool down again fixes that issue for a while. 

If you have defect memory or a mosfet, you not only need spare parts but also know what you are doing. 

In the case of a 780 you don't really have a lot to loose so give it a try. Look up videos on how disassemble that card and how to resolder processors. Shield the components around the processor with aluminum foil, as you don't want to heat components that don't need to be heated. 

Make sure you have something to clean the processor with and thermal paste for reassembling the card.

Usualy Radeon availability in our country is kinda bad (most go to Germany, and some other bigger countries). Last year, back at launch before prices went beserk, I was kinda interested in a 3060Ti, but felt the price was a bit... high with prices between 475 to 499 euro's (considering, back then, even 3070's went for around 500 to 600 euro's). The 3060Ti outperforms this quite a bit, and even the lower tier 3060 (non-ti) is more expensive now than the Ti was at launch.
The 6600XT and 3060 could have been okay-ish cards for their supposed prices (though the 6600 msrp still high), but at current prices they're bad value. But the only other option pretty much is a GT1030 (GDDR5 version), because anything else is way too overpriced (even the GTX 1650, which always had a bad reputation because of pricing, is almost 200 euro's more expensive than what it used to be).  If my current GPU would suddenly die, I think I'd go for a 1030 and wait and hope that at some point prices get more reasonable.

In other reviews, with high-res textures and high resolutions, it became clear that the 8GB 3060Ti and even the older 5700 XT had less trouble dealing with it than the 6600 XT did, both the other cards have bigger memory busses and so it's less of a problem. comments.text:
I don't know if anyone remembers me talking about it before, but I finally built my RyZen 5 1600AF system! I've mentioned before what GPU I was going to put into it. Yeah. I wish I could get something like a RX 6600XT in my system. Having said that, my GTX 970 is the best video card I've ever used in a PC, and I really enjoy it! The thing is, I got it secondhand. (for $80, so at least it was cheap.) It has some coil whine.

I'm running on a 1280x1024 monitor right now. I can only imagine how the coil whine will be once I get a proper 1080p monitor. I did the math. My monitor has roughly 63% of the pixels a 1080p screen would have. I'm pretty sure the GTX targeted 1080p gaming at 60 fps when it came out. I mean, the most graphically advanced game I have right now is either Doom (2016) or (if you can imagine this) Diablo 2 Resurrected.

I am not sure if the "shiny turd in my PC" applies in this case because it's simply the best video card I've ever owned. It has the coil whine, but it does work. I can't say the same for the RX 480 I got for $75 a year before I got the GTX 970.

Well, enough griping. I'll tell one more story about my computer build, then I'll list its specs for those who are curious.

This computer is built with mITX in mind. I got a mITX ASRock B450 Fatal1ty motherboard, which I'm pretty happy with for the CPU/GPU combination. I got a case with the mITX form factor, but it's actually fairly large. It can fit a radiator and water cooler, and has lots of room for a tower CPU cooler and several 2.5" and 3.5" drives, as well as an optical drive. With an RX 1600AF that I don't plan to overclock, I just stuck with the stock cooler.

To the point. The motherboard has its NVME M.2 drive slot on the bottom of the motherboard. I decided to get a 2TB Mushkin E-Pilot drive, which is somewhat high performance. I had no idea how hot it would run. I decided to get a heatsink for it, just to be safe. The standoffs for the motherboard didn't provide enough clearance for the drive and the heatsink. I decided I really wanted to use the heatsink, though.

I took the time to carefully mark out and measure the spot where the heatsink was resting and cut a hole in the bottom of my case so the heatsink would stick out. I managed to get the hole location and size perfect. It's just not as pretty as if I had been able to do it with a Dremel, which I don't own. (I used a drill, sheet metal shears, and filed down the rough edges.) So, yeah. Yay for my first case mod being a success!

Here's my PC:
RyZen 5 1600AF
EVGA GTX 970
EVGA 600W ATX PSU, (600BR or BQ, it's the semi-modular one)
Geil 3200 MHz Geil Memory (2x8 sticks for dual-channel)
M.2 2TB Mushkin E-Pilot NVME drive
Seagate Barracuda 4 TB mechanical drive
Some LG DVD Drive. I still have CDs to rip, you know.
ASRock B450 mITX Fatal1ty motherboard
Fractal Design M500 case

I spent more time on cable management with this build than I have any other, and it shows. I mean, it's still not the pretties you've ever seen. It's good, considering I only went semi-modular and didn't get completely custom power cables. I left the GPU cables really accessible and easy to remove in case I'm able to get a nice GPU. (Or, if this GTX 970 fails and I'm forced to install my Rx 560.)

Ok I've been seeing a lot of people complaining about prices and blaming amd for it.
Tldr
1. Amd is not making these GPUs in the first place

The board partners of amd like evga, msi, sapphire, etc... Who make the GPUs, are having prices of everything silicon increase, increasing the price of everything, components and boards. If they want to keep profiting they have to increase the price since you know supply and demand.

comments.text:
Limited as this card's RT capability is, I don't think you should discount it completely. At 1080p the 6600 XT can actually run most RT-enabled games at very playable rates (>60fps; I don't think anyone buying an entry-level GPU expects it to max out a 144Hz or better display, still in a few cases of very optimized RT games like Doom Eternal, the 6600 XT gets very close to that). Have in mind that almost all current RT games make limited use of raytracing effects because even a 3090 with DLSS is not good enough to do full path tracing for any game with complex geometry (i.e. excluding things like Minecraft or Quake RTX) at high resolution+fps. That will have to wait for another generation or two of hardware.

Second, even in games that already make relatively advanced use of RT such as Control, you can often get playable performance with dynamic resolution techniques. FSR is not useful specifically at 1080p, but Radeon cards aren't limited to the "official" FSR feature; they can often use alternatives like good implementations of TSSAA, or VRS which is also supported in hardware by the 6600 XT, perhaps in combination with FSR. These features are hit and miss, depending a lot of support by specific games, but you can typically count on them in the modern AAA titles that make the bulk of the titles used for GPU benchmarking.

comments.text:
@TheRedRaven_  No, gamers have been buying scalped GPUs. There’s a difference between a miner, and a mining farm. A mining farm usually has dozens of cards, whereas a miner can technically just have a CPU.

“Miners” aren’t evil, because it is a very, very small percentage of miners buying up the cards. The vast majority of individual GPU miners are people mining on whatever they already have.

Even small at-home farms are limited by their electrical.

Industrial mining farms have to compete with every GPU on the market. Old cards can mine too, and mining doesn’t damage cards (assuming you underclock the core and OC the memory)

Industrial mining operators buy as many cards as they can because their entire purpose and income derives from mining.

The average miner though is just making like 100usd a month on their gaming card.

When the mining craze came around, I just so happened to have a 2080ti, and rx580 and a 2060ko (I build PCs). I mine with those and have no plans to buy anymore cards because I’m not investing my main income into my secondary income, especially when I have no large-scale plan to get rid of any potential newly acquired hardware in the future.

The vast, vast, vast majority of miners are in my position. But we are the minority of the hashing power. Now, if everyone with a card capable of outputing like 15mh/s were to start mining, new single-card miners would literally be taking profits from industrial-scale mining operations (think hundreds or thousands of cards). Likewise, these industrial mining ops would see reduced profit and be more likely to dump their supply on the market, and certainly would not buy more.

comments.text:
Don't get me wrong, Jay. I love your channel(s) and builds. But the one thing you're missing here is this:

The 6600XT is a PCIE v4 x8 card.

If you plug it in to a PCIE v4 capable system, bandwidth between the CPU and the card are the same as a PCIE v3 x16. BUT if you have a PCIE v3 system, whether that's a limitation of the CPU or motherboard you purchased, this card will run as if it's stuffed into a PCIE v3 x8 slot. On VRAM- and CPU-intensive titles, this card is going to choke. This particular 'nerf' is inexcusable. It completely prevents the card from delivering $400 performance in any situation that isn't a PCIE v4 system pushing a 1080p monitor. 

Indeed - these are the types of architecture nerfs we used to see in sub $125 cards. Even when compared to a RTX 3060 - which this card outperforms when installed in a PCIE v4 system, the 3060 won't lose as much steam on the higher-end games because they kept the 256-bit memory bus and x16 PCIE bandwidth.

In my honest opinion, this is a $175 card. Period. Maybe as high as $225 for an 'Extreme Overclock' version.

Keeping the card a PCIE x16 with at least a 196-bit memory bus could have made it a compelling $350 card. But no. AMD went for the money-grab in a stressed market. Consumers who get shit on like this remember it.  And when the market reverses and demand falls to more 'normal' levels', this kind of consumer treatment will be remembered and it won't translate into 'repeat buyers.'

Thanks for the video. I'm pissed at AMD bro, not you.

I, just like many others would love to see high performance GFX cards at extremely low prices. However, there has been a shift in the market, and to be fair to that market (this regarding MSRP, not scalped prices) the 6600XT is on-par performance wise with a 1080Ti. 4 years ago that level of performance cost me 800, now it's available for 375. The big conglomorates have been leveraging this metric, as opposed to the metric of naming convention "tier" class of card it seems. That said, these cards are widely available here at this price point. The 3060Ti is still around 575 here, and available. Given the 3060Ti is around 25% (+) faster than the 1080Ti and considering that cards price at launch .. well, you get the idea.

This appears to be inflation and market shift, it's even happened for other things .. a bar of chocolate when I was a kid (which appear smaller these days, or maybe it's just because I am bigger now) costs around 10x the price, if not a lot more, even milk is more expensive now for the same volume compared to 2017; that volume hasn't halved in price.

Anyway, I think the real issue here is twofold; the top end prices are astronomical, and there is a risk PC gaming will be priced out of the market and into extinction compared to the price of consoles. So overall the first issue, of high price top tier cards, may well result in these companies actually pricing themselves into extinction. Just my perspective.

If you're willing to pay a lot and get something good you probably will be able to soon or now (like if a 3080 was going to be your target anyway), but if you were previously in the "I'll buy a half-decent card for under $300 every couple of gens" crowd, it's still going to be a while.

comments.text:
Honestly, if you've got a card that's not about to fail and not holding you back from enjoying games you want to play, keep it and save that money for a couple of years.  Even if it's not up to 1080p60fps on everything.

Individually, it doesn't really matter that much that I'm sticking with my R9 270X or whatever it is (it's been so long I've literally forgotten the last 3 characters - I know it's an R9 200 series), but if 5% of the people who are looking for graphics cards can just stick with their current solution until the supply/demand situation stabilizes, the demand goes down by 5% and makes it 5% easier for manufacturers to meet that supply shortage.  Price gouging and scalping end a little bit faster, and that 5% have money in the bank to jump back into the market as soon as things are more normal.

(Of course, this only works so much.  If 50% of the market did that, prices would appear to stabilize much faster, because meeting half the demand is much easier than meeting all of it...but then the other half of the demand jumps in at once and completely destabilizes everything again.  Supply and Demand situations, when stable, have a bit of a buffer - there's always a bit more supply than there is to meet demand, so retailers don't go out of stock and present a perceived shortage. For things as complex as graphics cards, that margin for error is never very large - even my 5% hypothetical group would likely cause ripples in the market if they acted all at once.  50% would throw us right back into critical levels of shortage again.)

I can get 90-120+ fps @1080p on my elderly gpu (r9 390) for the time being, so i upgraded my monitor from a 60hz one to a freesync display with a refresh rate of 165hz and the difference is night and day. On the 60hz screen i either had to use triple buffering vsync and deal with slight input lag, or unlock the framerate and deal with constant, distracting sceeen tearing. With triple buffer vsync occasionally i would dip to like 45-52 fps for a sec. Which doesn't matter if youre looting drawers in Fallout at your own pace, but matters a lot if you play doom eternal on nightmare and UN. I would always notice every one of those brief dips. Freesync and a higher refresh rate lets me uncap the framerate, never dip below 60 anymore and often have much higher than 60. Everything feels much more responsive and fluid and I'm able to swap weapons more quickly which means im able to deal damage more quickly. I'm pretty good at the game but im no speedrunner or professional gamer and i don't need to be to feel the benefits of a higher framerate. Framerate is much less important in other games, and playing at a locked 60fps wouldn't matter if i just wanted to play doom eternal on normal. So more than 60 might indeed be pointless for your needs but when reaction time is very important or mechanics are tied to framerate like DEs swap speed then higher fps is absolutely not a gimmick
